282: +
283:  ### AP-01: Phantom Color
284: +
285:  **Description**: Outputting a hex color value that does not exist in the extracted `tokens.json` or style data. Often caused by rounding, autocomplete, or confusing similarly-named values.
286: +
287:  **Bad Example**:
288:  ```markdown
289:  | Role    | Value   |
290:  |---------|---------|
291:  | Primary | #2563eb |
292:  ```
293: +
294:  **Why It's Wrong**: The actual extracted token was `#2564eb`. A one-digit difference creates a color that was never present in the source design. Downstream consumers (code generators, theme builders) will produce output that diverges from the real product.
295: +
296:  **Correct Approach**:
297:  ```markdown
298:  | Role    | Value   |
299: @@ -39,19 +57,24 @@ A catalog of common mistakes when generating DESIGN.md files from extracted desi
300:  | Primary | #2564eb |
301:  ```
302:  Always copy hex values verbatim from the extracted data. Never round, correct, or "normalize" color values to well-known palette values.
303: +
304:  **Detection**: Diff every hex value in the output against the source token file. Any value absent from the source is a phantom.
305:  
306:  ---
307:  
308:  ### AP-02: Generic Description
309: +
310:  **Description**: Using vague, meaningless adjectives to describe the design system instead of concrete, measurable characteristics.
311: +
312:  **Bad Example**:
313:  ```markdown
314:  ## Overview
315:  The application uses a clean and modern design with a professional color palette
316:  and elegant typography choices.
317:  ```
318: +
319:  **Why It's Wrong**: "Clean", "modern", "professional", and "elegant" carry zero actionable information. They describe every design system ever created and distinguish nothing. A code generator cannot act on these words.
320: +
321:  **Correct Approach**:
322:  ```markdown
323:  ## Overview
324: @@ -60,30 +83,38 @@ The application uses a high-contrast light theme with a single accent hue
325:  weight stops (400-700) with a 1.25 type scale. Spacing follows an 8px base grid.
326:  ```
327:  Replace every adjective with a specific value, ratio, or named convention.
328: +
329:  **Detection**: Search the output for these banned terms: clean, modern, elegant, professional, sleek, beautiful, stunning, polished, sophisticated, minimalist (when used as a standalone descriptor without supporting metrics).
330:  
331:  ---
332:  
333:  ### AP-03: Semantic Misattribution
334: +
335:  **Description**: Labeling a color as "primary" based on its hue (e.g., blue = primary) rather than its actual usage frequency and role in the interface.
336: +
337:  **Bad Example**:
338:  ```markdown
339:  - Primary: #2564eb (blue)
340:  - Secondary: #6b7280 (gray)
341:  ```
342: +
343:  **Why It's Wrong**: If `#6b7280` appears on 80% of text and UI surfaces while `#2564eb` appears only on 3 buttons, then gray is functionally the dominant color. Calling the rarely-used blue "primary" misleads theme generation and creates incorrect weight in the output system.
344: +
345:  **Correct Approach**:
346:  ```markdown
347:  - Text/UI Base: #6b7280 (gray) — used across body text, labels, borders; highest frequency
348:  - Action Accent: #2564eb (blue) — used on CTAs and active states; low frequency, high salience
349:  ```
350:  Assign semantic roles based on measured frequency and functional role, not on hue conventions.
351: +
352:  **Detection**: Cross-reference the semantic label with frequency data. If a color labeled "primary" ranks below 3rd in usage frequency, flag it.
353:

356:  ### AP-04: Missing Interaction States
357: +
358:  **Description**: Documenting only the default/rest state of interactive elements and omitting hover, focus, active, and disabled states.
359: +
360:  **Bad Example**:
361:  ```markdown
362:  ## Buttons
363: @@ -92,7 +123,9 @@ Assign semantic roles based on measured frequency and functional role, not on hu
364:  - Border radius: 6px
365:  - Padding: 8px 16px
366:  ```
367: +
368:  **Why It's Wrong**: A button specification without interaction states is incomplete. Any implementation built from this spec will either invent states (introducing inconsistency) or ship without them (failing accessibility and UX).
369: +
370:  **Correct Approach**:
371:  ```markdown
372:  ## Buttons
373: @@ -108,18 +141,23 @@ Assign semantic roles based on measured frequency and functional role, not on hu
374:  - Padding: 8px 16px
375:  ```
376:  Document every state present in the extracted data. If the source data lacks states, note the gap explicitly rather than omitting silently.
377: +
378:  **Detection**: For every interactive component (button, link, input, toggle, checkbox), verify that at least hover and focus states are documented.

381:  
382:  ### AP-05: Over-inference
383: +
384:  **Description**: Extrapolating a design principle or pattern from a single occurrence or low-frequency observation.
385: +
386:  **Bad Example**:
387:  ```markdown
388:  ## Design Principles
389:  - All cards use a left blue accent border to indicate importance hierarchy.
390:  ```
391: +
392:  **Why It's Wrong**: If only 1 out of 14 cards in the extracted data has a left blue border, this is not a system-wide principle. It may be a one-off treatment for a specific context. Elevating it to a principle causes over-application in generated output.
393: +
394:  **Correct Approach**:
395:  ```markdown
396:  ## Card Variants
397: @@ -127,12 +165,15 @@ Document every state present in the extracted data. If the source data lacks sta
398:  - **Highlighted card** (1 occurrence): Adds left 3px #2564eb border accent
399:  ```
400:  State the frequency. Distinguish one-off treatments from system patterns. A pattern requires at minimum 3 consistent occurrences to be stated as a convention.
401: +
402:  **Detection**: Every stated "principle" or "always" claim should have a frequency annotation. If the backing data shows fewer than 3 instances, demote from principle to variant note.

406:  ### AP-06: Format Inconsistency
407: +
408:  **Description**: Mixing incompatible formats for the same type of value within the document.
409: +
410:  **Bad Example**:
411:  ```markdown
412:  - Background: #FFF
413: @@ -142,7 +183,9 @@ State the frequency. Distinguish one-off treatments from system patterns. A patt
414:  - Font weight: bold
415:  - Heading weight: 700
416:  ```
417: +
418:  **Why It's Wrong**: Inconsistent casing (`#FFF` vs `#2564EB`), mixed notation (`hex` vs `rgb`), and mixed weight formats (`bold` vs `700`) make the document unreliable for programmatic consumption. Parsers and theme generators will choke or produce inconsistent results.
419: +
420:  **Correct Approach**:
421:  ```markdown
422:  - Background: #ffffff
423: @@ -153,12 +196,15 @@ State the frequency. Distinguish one-off treatments from system patterns. A patt
424:  - Heading weight: 700
425:  ```
426:  Pick one format per value type and enforce it: lowercase 6-digit hex for colors, numeric values for font weights, px for absolute sizes, rem for relative sizes.
427: +
428:  **Detection**: Regex scan for mixed hex formats (`#[A-F]` mixed with `#[a-f]`, or 3-digit mixed with 6-digit), mixed color notations, or `bold`/`normal` mixed with numeric weights.

433: +
434:  **Description**: Documenting heading and body text levels but omitting monospace/code font, caption, overline, or other specialized type levels present in the data.
435: +
436:  **Bad Example**:
437:  ```markdown
438:  ## Typography Scale
439: @@ -170,7 +216,9 @@ Pick one format per value type and enforce it: lowercase 6-digit hex for colors,
440:  | Body  | 16px | 400    | Inter      |
441:  | Small | 14px | 400    | Inter      |

446:  **Correct Approach**:
447:  ```markdown

450:  | Code     | 14px | 400    | JetBrains Mono  | 1.6         |

452:  Include every distinct type treatment found in the data, including code, caption, overline, and label levels.
453: +
454:  **Detection**: Search extracted data for font-family values not represented in the typography table. Check for monospace fonts specifically.

458:  ### AP-08: Meaningless Don'ts
459: +
460:  **Description**: Stating prohibitions that are too vague to be actionable by a human or machine.
461: +
462:  **Bad Example**:
463:  ```markdown
464:  ## Don'ts
465: @@ -198,7 +249,9 @@ Include every distinct type treatment found in the data, including code, caption
466:  - Don't make text too small
467:  - Don't overcrowd the layout
468:  ```
469: +
470:  **Why It's Wrong**: "Too many" is undefined. "Too small" is undefined. "Overcrowd" is undefined. No system or person can evaluate compliance with these rules. They occupy space without constraining anything.

473:  ```markdown

475: @@ -207,12 +260,15 @@ Include every distinct type treatment found in the data, including code, caption
476:  - Maintain minimum 16px gap between adjacent interactive elements (touch target spacing)
477:  ```
478:  Every constraint must include a threshold, value, or enumerable condition.
479: +

484:  ### AP-09: Non-Self-Contained Prompts
485: +
486:  **Description**: Writing an agent prompt section that references tokens by semantic name without including the actual values, requiring the agent to look elsewhere in the document.
487: +
488:  **Bad Example**:
489:  ```markdown
490:  ## Agent Prompt
491: @@ -220,7 +276,9 @@ When generating UI, use the primary color for call-to-action buttons and the
492:  secondary color for less prominent actions. Apply the standard border radius
493:  to all interactive elements.
494:  ```
495: +
496:  **Why It's Wrong**: An LLM consuming this prompt in isolation (e.g., as a system message) has no idea what "the primary color" resolves to. It will hallucinate a value. The prompt must be self-contained.
497: +
498:  **Correct Approach**:
499:  ```markdown
500:  ## Agent Prompt
501: @@ -231,12 +289,15 @@ When generating UI, apply these exact values:
502:  - Focus ring: 0 0 0 3px rgba(37,100,235,0.3)
503:  ```
504:  Inline every referenced value directly in the prompt. The prompt must function correctly even if extracted from the document and used standalone.
505: +
506:  **Detection**: Search the agent prompt section for semantic color names (primary, secondary, accent, etc.) or relative references (the standard, the default) without an accompanying literal value on the same line.

510:  ### AP-10: Shadow-Border Confusion
511: +
512:  **Description**: Classifying a zero-blur box-shadow used as a border substitute as an "elevation shadow," conflating two distinct visual techniques.
513: +
514:  **Bad Example**:
515:  ```markdown
516:  ## Elevation
517: @@ -246,7 +307,9 @@ Inline every referenced value directly in the prompt. The prompt must function c
518:  | Medium| 0 4px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.1)    |
519:  | High  | 0 10px 15px rgba(0,0,0,0.1)  |
520:  ```
521: +
522:  **Why It's Wrong**: `0 0 0 1px` has no offset and no blur; it renders as a 1px solid border. Grouping it with elevation shadows misrepresents its visual function and causes agents to apply border-like effects when elevation is requested.
523: +
524:  **Correct Approach**:
525:  ```markdown
526:  ## Borders
527: @@ -261,12 +324,15 @@ Inline every referenced value directly in the prompt. The prompt must function c
528:  | High   | 0 10px 15px rgba(0,0,0,0.1)      |
529:  ```
530:  Separate zero-blur box-shadows into a border section. Only shadows with non-zero blur or offset belong in elevation.
531: +
532:  **Detection**: In the elevation/shadow table, flag any entry where both X-offset, Y-offset, and blur are zero (pattern: `0 0 0 Npx`).

563: +
564:  **Description**: Using generic indexed names like "Blue 1" or "Gray Light" that carry no functional meaning and create ambiguity.

566:  **Bad Example**:

571:  - Gray Dark: #374151

615: +
616:  **Description**: Referring to the same design token by different names in different sections of the document.

768:  ### AP-20: Ignoring Framework Context
769: +
770:  **Description**: Failing to mention the detected CSS framework (Tailwind, Bootstrap, Material UI, etc.) or misrepresenting utility classes as custom CSS.

772:  **Bad Example**:
773:  ```markdown
774:  ## Styling
775: @@ -511,7 +622,9 @@ The application uses custom CSS with consistent spacing and color application.

281: +## 2. ANTI-PATTERN CATALOG
282: +
283:  ### AP-01: Phantom Color
284: +
285:  **Description**: Outputting a hex color value that does not exist in the extracted `tokens.json` or style data. Often caused by rounding, autocomplete, or confusing similarly-named values.
286: +
287:  **Bad Example**:
288:  ```markdown
289:  | Role    | Value   |
290:  |---------|---------|
291:  | Primary | #2563eb |
292:  ```
293: +
294:  **Why It's Wrong**: The actual extracted token was `#2564eb`. A one-digit difference creates a color that was never present in the source design. Downstream consumers (code generators, theme builders) will produce output that diverges from the real product.
295: +
296:  **Correct Approach**:
297:  ```markdown
298:  | Role    | Value   |
299: @@ -39,19 +57,24 @@ A catalog of common mistakes when generating DESIGN.md files from extracted desi
300:  | Primary | #2564eb |
301:  ```
302:  Always copy hex values verbatim from the extracted data. Never round, correct, or "normalize" color values to well-known palette values.
303: +
304:  **Detection**: Diff every hex value in the output against the source token file. Any value absent from the source is a phantom.
305:

307:  
308:  ### AP-02: Generic Description
309: +
310:  **Description**: Using vague, meaningless adjectives to describe the design system instead of concrete, measurable characteristics.
311: +
312:  **Bad Example**:
313:  ```markdown
314:  ## Overview
315:  The application uses a clean and modern design with a professional color palette
316:  and elegant typography choices.
317:  ```
318: +
319:  **Why It's Wrong**: "Clean", "modern", "professional", and "elegant" carry zero actionable information. They describe every design system ever created and distinguish nothing. A code generator cannot act on these words.
320: +
321:  **Correct Approach**:
322:  ```markdown
323:  ## Overview
324: @@ -60,30 +83,38 @@ The application uses a high-contrast light theme with a single accent hue
325:  weight stops (400-700) with a 1.25 type scale. Spacing follows an 8px base grid.
326:  ```
327:  Replace every adjective with a specific value, ratio, or named convention.
328: +
329:  **Detection**: Search the output for these banned terms: clean, modern, elegant, professional, sleek, beautiful, stunning, polished, sophisticated, minimalist (when used as a standalone descriptor without supporting metrics).
330:  
331:  ---
332:  
333:  ### AP-03: Semantic Misattribution
334: +
335:  **Description**: Labeling a color as "primary" based on its hue (e.g., blue = primary) rather than its actual usage frequency and role in the interface.
336: +
337:  **Bad Example**:
338:  ```markdown
339:  - Primary: #2564eb (blue)
340:  - Secondary: #6b7280 (gray)
341:  ```
342: +
343:  **Why It's Wrong**: If `#6b7280` appears on 80% of text and UI surfaces while `#2564eb` appears only on 3 buttons, then gray is functionally the dominant color. Calling the rarely-used blue "primary" misleads theme generation and creates incorrect weight in the output system.
344: +
345:  **Correct Approach**:
346:  ```markdown
347:  - Text/UI Base: #6b7280 (gray) — used across body text, labels, borders; highest frequency
348:  - Action Accent: #2564eb (blue) — used on CTAs and active states; low frequency, high salience
349:  ```
350:  Assign semantic roles based on measured frequency and functional role, not on hue conventions.
351: +
352:  **Detection**: Cross-reference the semantic label with frequency data. If a color labeled "primary" ranks below 3rd in usage frequency, flag it.
353:

356:  ### AP-04: Missing Interaction States
357: +
358:  **Description**: Documenting only the default/rest state of interactive elements and omitting hover, focus, active, and disabled states.
359: +
360:  **Bad Example**:
361:  ```markdown
362:  ## Buttons
363: @@ -92,7 +123,9 @@ Assign semantic roles based on measured frequency and functional role, not on hu
364:  - Border radius: 6px
365:  - Padding: 8px 16px
366:  ```
367: +
368:  **Why It's Wrong**: A button specification without interaction states is incomplete. Any implementation built from this spec will either invent states (introducing inconsistency) or ship without them (failing accessibility and UX).
369: +
370:  **Correct Approach**:
371:  ```markdown
372:  ## Buttons
373: @@ -108,18 +141,23 @@ Assign semantic roles based on measured frequency and functional role, not on hu
374:  - Padding: 8px 16px
375:  ```
376:  Document every state present in the extracted data. If the source data lacks states, note the gap explicitly rather than omitting silently.
377: +
378:  **Detection**: For every interactive component (button, link, input, toggle, checkbox), verify that at least hover and focus states are documented.
379:

381:  
382:  ### AP-05: Over-inference
383: +
384:  **Description**: Extrapolating a design principle or pattern from a single occurrence or low-frequency observation.
385: +
386:  **Bad Example**:
387:  ```markdown
388:  ## Design Principles
389:  - All cards use a left blue accent border to indicate importance hierarchy.
390:  ```
391: +
392:  **Why It's Wrong**: If only 1 out of 14 cards in the extracted data has a left blue border, this is not a system-wide principle. It may be a one-off treatment for a specific context. Elevating it to a principle causes over-application in generated output.
393: +
394:  **Correct Approach**:
395:  ```markdown
396:  ## Card Variants
397: @@ -127,12 +165,15 @@ Document every state present in the extracted data. If the source data lacks sta
398:  - **Highlighted card** (1 occurrence): Adds left 3px #2564eb border accent
399:  ```
400:  State the frequency. Distinguish one-off treatments from system patterns. A pattern requires at minimum 3 consistent occurrences to be stated as a convention.
401: +
402:  **Detection**: Every stated "principle" or "always" claim should have a frequency annotation. If the backing data shows fewer than 3 instances, demote from principle to variant note.
403:

405:  
406:  ### AP-06: Format Inconsistency
407: +
408:  **Description**: Mixing incompatible formats for the same type of value within the document.
409: +
410:  **Bad Example**:
411:  ```markdown
412:  - Background: #FFF
413: @@ -142,7 +183,9 @@ State the frequency. Distinguish one-off treatments from system patterns. A patt
414:  - Font weight: bold
415:  - Heading weight: 700
416:  ```
417: +
418:  **Why It's Wrong**: Inconsistent casing (`#FFF` vs `#2564EB`), mixed notation (`hex` vs `rgb`), and mixed weight formats (`bold` vs `700`) make the document unreliable for programmatic consumption. Parsers and theme generators will choke or produce inconsistent results.
419: +
420:  **Correct Approach**:
421:  ```markdown
422:  - Background: #ffffff
423: @@ -153,12 +196,15 @@ State the frequency. Distinguish one-off treatments from system patterns. A patt
424:  - Heading weight: 700
425:  ```
426:  Pick one format per value type and enforce it: lowercase 6-digit hex for colors, numeric values for font weights, px for absolute sizes, rem for relative sizes.
427: +
428:  **Detection**: Regex scan for mixed hex formats (`#[A-F]` mixed with `#[a-f]`, or 3-digit mixed with 6-digit), mixed color notations, or `bold`/`normal` mixed with numeric weights.
429:

432:  ### AP-07: Typography Table Gaps
433: +
434:  **Description**: Documenting heading and body text levels but omitting monospace/code font, caption, overline, or other specialized type levels present in the data.
435: +
436:  **Bad Example**:
437:  ```markdown
438:  ## Typography Scale
439: @@ -170,7 +216,9 @@ Pick one format per value type and enforce it: lowercase 6-digit hex for colors,
440:  | Body  | 16px | 400    | Inter      |
441:  | Small | 14px | 400    | Inter      |
442:  ```
443: +
444:  **Why It's Wrong**: If the extracted data includes a monospace font (e.g., `JetBrains Mono` at 14px/400 used in code blocks), omitting it leaves a gap that implementers will fill with arbitrary choices.
445: +
446:  **Correct Approach**:
447:  ```markdown
448:  ## Typography Scale
449: @@ -185,12 +233,15 @@ Pick one format per value type and enforce it: lowercase 6-digit hex for colors,
450:  | Code     | 14px | 400    | JetBrains Mono  | 1.6         |
451:  ```
452:  Include every distinct type treatment found in the data, including code, caption, overline, and label levels.
453: +
454:  **Detection**: Search extracted data for font-family values not represented in the typography table. Check for monospace fonts specifically.

458:  ### AP-08: Meaningless Don'ts
459: +
460:  **Description**: Stating prohibitions that are too vague to be actionable by a human or machine.
461: +
462:  **Bad Example**:
463:  ```markdown
464:  ## Don'ts
465: @@ -198,7 +249,9 @@ Include every distinct type treatment found in the data, including code, caption
466:  - Don't make text too small
467:  - Don't overcrowd the layout
468:  ```
469: +
470:  **Why It's Wrong**: "Too many" is undefined. "Too small" is undefined. "Overcrowd" is undefined. No system or person can evaluate compliance with these rules. They occupy space without constraining anything.
471: +
472:  **Correct Approach**:
473:  ```markdown
474:  ## Constraints
475: @@ -207,12 +260,15 @@ Include every distinct type treatment found in the data, including code, caption
476:  - Maintain minimum 16px gap between adjacent interactive elements (touch target spacing)
477:  ```
478:  Every constraint must include a threshold, value, or enumerable condition.
479: +
480:  **Detection**: Flag any "Don't" entry that lacks a numeric value, specific color, named element, or testable condition.
481:

483:  
484:  ### AP-09: Non-Self-Contained Prompts
485: +
486:  **Description**: Writing an agent prompt section that references tokens by semantic name without including the actual values, requiring the agent to look elsewhere in the document.
487: +
488:  **Bad Example**:
489:  ```markdown
490:  ## Agent Prompt
491: @@ -220,7 +276,9 @@ When generating UI, use the primary color for call-to-action buttons and the
492:  secondary color for less prominent actions. Apply the standard border radius
493:  to all interactive elements.
494:  ```
495: +
496:  **Why It's Wrong**: An LLM consuming this prompt in isolation (e.g., as a system message) has no idea what "the primary color" resolves to. It will hallucinate a value. The prompt must be self-contained.
497: +
498:  **Correct Approach**:
499:  ```markdown
500:  ## Agent Prompt
501: @@ -231,12 +289,15 @@ When generating UI, apply these exact values:
502:  - Focus ring: 0 0 0 3px rgba(37,100,235,0.3)
503:  ```
504:  Inline every referenced value directly in the prompt. The prompt must function correctly even if extracted from the document and used standalone.
505: +
506:  **Detection**: Search the agent prompt section for semantic color names (primary, secondary, accent, etc.) or relative references (the standard, the default) without an accompanying literal value on the same line.
507:

510:  ### AP-10: Shadow-Border Confusion
511: +
512:  **Description**: Classifying a zero-blur box-shadow used as a border substitute as an "elevation shadow," conflating two distinct visual techniques.
513: +
514:  **Bad Example**:
515:  ```markdown
516:  ## Elevation
517: @@ -246,7 +307,9 @@ Inline every referenced value directly in the prompt. The prompt must function c
518:  | Medium| 0 4px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.1)    |
519:  | High  | 0 10px 15px rgba(0,0,0,0.1)  |
520:  ```
521: +
522:  **Why It's Wrong**: `0 0 0 1px` has no offset and no blur; it renders as a 1px solid border. Grouping it with elevation shadows misrepresents its visual function and causes agents to apply border-like effects when elevation is requested.
523: +
524:  **Correct Approach**:
525:  ```markdown
526:  ## Borders
527: @@ -261,12 +324,15 @@ Inline every referenced value directly in the prompt. The prompt must function c
528:  | High   | 0 10px 15px rgba(0,0,0,0.1)      |
529:  ```
530:  Separate zero-blur box-shadows into a border section. Only shadows with non-zero blur or offset belong in elevation.
531: +
532:  **Detection**: In the elevation/shadow table, flag any entry where both X-offset, Y-offset, and blur are zero (pattern: `0 0 0 Npx`).
533:

536:  ### AP-11: Dark Mode Omission
537: +
538:  **Description**: Failing to document dark mode color mappings when the extracted data clearly contains them.
539: +
540:  **Bad Example**:
541:  ```markdown
542:  ## Color Palette
543: @@ -277,7 +343,9 @@ Separate zero-blur box-shadows into a border section. Only shadows with non-zero
544:  | Surface    | #f9fafb |
545:  ```
546:  *(No mention of dark mode despite tokens.json containing `dark.background: #0f172a`, etc.)*
547: +
548:  **Why It's Wrong**: Ignoring dark mode data produces a DESIGN.md that only works for light theme. Agents generating dark-mode UI will invent colors rather than using the documented values.
549: +
550:  **Correct Approach**:
551:  ```markdown
552:  ## Color Palette
553: @@ -289,12 +357,15 @@ Separate zero-blur box-shadows into a border section. Only shadows with non-zero
554:  | Border     | #e5e7eb | #334155 |
555:  ```
556:  If the source data contains dark/light variants, always present both in a single table.
557: +
558:  **Detection**: Search the source data for keys containing "dark", "night", or theme-variant identifiers. If present but not reflected in the output, flag the omission.

562:  ### AP-12: Vague Color Names
563: +
564:  **Description**: Using generic indexed names like "Blue 1" or "Gray Light" that carry no functional meaning and create ambiguity.
565: +
566:  **Bad Example**:
567:  ```markdown
568:  ## Colors
569: @@ -304,7 +375,9 @@ If the source data contains dark/light variants, always present both in a single
570:  - Gray Light: #f9fafb
571:  - Gray Dark: #374151
572:  ```
573: +
574:  **Why It's Wrong**: "Blue 1" and "Blue 2" give no indication of when to use which. An implementer or agent must guess. Sequential numbering provides ordering but not purpose.
575: +
576:  **Correct Approach**:
577:  ```markdown
578:  ## Colors
579: @@ -315,12 +388,15 @@ If the source data contains dark/light variants, always present both in a single
580:  - Text Secondary: #374151 — supporting body text, labels
581:  ```
582:  Each name should encode its function (where/when it is used), not just its hue and relative lightness.
583: +
584:  **Detection**: Flag color names that are purely `{Hue} {Number}` or `{Hue} {Relative}` without a functional descriptor.

588:  ### AP-13: Key Characteristics Without Values
589: +
590:  **Description**: Stating a design characteristic as a qualitative observation without the specific values that define it.
591: +
592:  **Bad Example**:
593:  ```markdown
594:  ## Key Characteristics
595: @@ -328,7 +404,9 @@ Each name should encode its function (where/when it is used), not just its hue a
596:  - Large, bold headings
597:  - Subtle borders between sections
598:  ```
599: +
600:  **Why It's Wrong**: "Tight" could mean 4px or 12px. "Large" could mean 24px or 48px. "Subtle" could mean 0.5px solid #eee or 1px solid rgba(0,0,0,0.05). Without values, these statements are useless for implementation.
601: +
602:  **Correct Approach**:
603:  ```markdown
604:  ## Key Characteristics
605: @@ -337,12 +415,15 @@ Each name should encode its function (where/when it is used), not just its hue a
606:  - Section dividers: 1px solid #e5e7eb (light mode), 1px solid #334155 (dark mode)
607:  ```
608:  Every characteristic must include the measured value from the extracted data.
609: +
610:  **Detection**: Flag any bullet point in a characteristics or principles section that lacks at least one numeric value (px, rem, hex, percentage, ratio).

614:  ### AP-14: Cross-Section Terminology Drift
615: +
616:  **Description**: Referring to the same design token by different names in different sections of the document.
617: +
618:  **Bad Example**:
619:  ```markdown
620:  ## Section 2: Color Palette
621: @@ -354,7 +435,9 @@ Every characteristic must include the measured value from the extracted data.
622:  ## Section 9: Agent Prompt
623:  Apply the Main Blue for interactive elements.
624:  ```
625: +
626:  **Why It's Wrong**: "Primary Blue", "Brand Blue", and "Main Blue" all reference `#2564eb`, but an agent or reader cannot be sure they are the same without checking hex values. Inconsistent naming erodes trust in the document and causes duplication in generated code.
627: +
628:  **Correct Approach**:
629:  ```markdown
630:  ## Section 2: Color Palette
631: @@ -367,12 +450,15 @@ Apply the Main Blue for interactive elements.
632:  Interactive element background: #2564eb (Action Default)
633:  ```
634:  Choose one canonical name per token and use it consistently across every section. Always parenthetically include the hex value on first use in each section.
635: +
636:  **Detection**: Extract all semantic color names and their hex values. Group by hex value. If any hex value maps to more than one name, flag the drift.

640:  ### AP-15: Do's Without Specifics
641: +
642:  **Description**: Listing "Do" guidelines that restate a principle without specifying the exact values to apply.
643: +
644:  **Bad Example**:
645:  ```markdown
646:  ## Do's
647: @@ -380,7 +466,9 @@ Choose one canonical name per token and use it consistently across every section
648:  - Maintain visual hierarchy with font sizes
649:  - Apply the brand colors consistently
650:  ```
651: +
652:  **Why It's Wrong**: Every design system aims for "consistent spacing." This tells the reader nothing about which spacing values constitute consistency in this specific system. It is a tautology.
653: +
654:  **Correct Approach**:
655:  ```markdown
656:  ## Do's
657: @@ -389,12 +477,15 @@ Choose one canonical name per token and use it consistently across every section
658:  - Limit accent color (#2564eb) to interactive elements and active indicators
659:  ```
660:  Every "Do" must reference specific values, tokens, or enumerable conditions from the design data.
661: +
662:  **Detection**: Flag any "Do" entry that contains words like "consistent", "appropriate", "proper", or "correct" without accompanying numeric values or token references.

666:  ### AP-16: Redundant Information
667: +
668:  **Description**: Restating information from a table in prose immediately below it, adding no new context.
669: +
670:  **Bad Example**:
671:  ```markdown
672:  ## Spacing Scale
673: @@ -409,7 +500,9 @@ Every "Do" must reference specific values, tokens, or enumerable conditions from
674:  The spacing scale uses 5 levels. The smallest is 4px (xs), followed by 8px (sm),
675:  then 16px (md), 24px (lg), and the largest at 32px (xl).
676:  ```
677: +
678:  **Why It's Wrong**: The prose adds zero information beyond what the table already states. It wastes tokens, increases document length, and creates a maintenance burden where two representations must be kept in sync.
679: +
680:  **Correct Approach**:
681:  ```markdown
682:  ## Spacing Scale
683: @@ -424,12 +517,15 @@ then 16px (md), 24px (lg), and the largest at 32px (xl).
684:  Base unit: 4px. The scale doubles at each major step (4 → 8 → 16 → 32) with 24px as an intermediate for component-level gaps.
685:  ```
686:  Prose following a table should add context, rationale, or relationships not visible in the table itself.
687: +
688:  **Detection**: Compare prose sentences to table content. If more than 80% of the prose is a direct restatement of table values, flag it as redundant.

692:  ### AP-17: Wrong Component Classification
693: +
694:  **Description**: Misclassifying a UI element, most commonly calling a styled anchor/link a "button variant" or a chip/tag a "badge."
695: +
696:  **Bad Example**:
697:  ```markdown
698:  ## Button Variants
699: @@ -437,7 +533,9 @@ Prose following a table should add context, rationale, or relationships not visi
700:  - Secondary Button: transparent background, #2564eb text, #2564eb border
701:  - Text Button: no background, #2564eb text, underline on hover
702:  ```
703: +
704:  **Why It's Wrong**: A "Text Button" with underline on hover is semantically and functionally a link (`<a>`), not a button (`<button>`). Misclassifying it causes agents to generate `<button>` elements where `<a>` is correct, harming accessibility and SEO.
705: +
706:  **Correct Approach**:
707:  ```markdown
708:  ## Buttons
709: @@ -449,18 +547,23 @@ Prose following a table should add context, rationale, or relationships not visi
710:  - Standalone Link: #2564eb text, no underline at rest, underline on hover
711:  ```
712:  Classify elements by their semantic role (navigates vs. performs action) and HTML element, not by visual similarity.
713: +
714:  **Detection**: Check for "button" entries that mention underline behavior or entries that describe navigation as their function.

719: +
720:  **Description**: Describing a complex multi-stop or angled gradient with a vague label like "blue gradient" instead of the full gradient definition.

722:  **Bad Example**:
723:  ```markdown
724:  ## Hero Section
725:  - Background: blue gradient
726:  ```

729: +
730:  **Correct Approach**:
731:  ```markdown

733: @@ -468,12 +571,15 @@ Classify elements by their semantic role (navigates vs. performs action) and HTM
734:  - Fallback solid: #2564eb
735:  ```
736:  Always include the full gradient definition: type, angle/direction, each color stop with position.
737: +

743: +
744:  **Description**: Describing layout structure with qualitative terms instead of concrete grid specifications.

846:  **Description**: Documenting colors, typography, and components without stating WCAG conformance level, contrast ratios, focus specifications, or touch target requirements.

870:  ### AP-24: State Blindness
871: +
872:  **Description**: Documenting only the default/resting state of components, ignoring loading, empty, error, disabled, and success states.
873: +
874:  **Bad Example**:
875:  ```markdown
876:  ## Data Table
877:  Background: #ffffff | Header: #f9fafb | Border: 1px solid #e5e7eb

879:  ```

881:  **Why It's Wrong**: A data table is empty when filtered results return nothing, loading when fetching, errored when the API fails, and may show selected rows. Documenting only the data-present state means implementers will invent the other states, creating visual inconsistency.

883:  **Correct Approach**:
884:  ```markdown

887:  | Row hover | Background #f9fafb |
888:  | Row selected | Background #eff6ff, left border 2px solid #3b82f6 |

1052:  ### AP-32: Value Invention from a Vague Token (v3)
1053: +
1054:  **Description**: Concretizing a vague or relative token value into a specific absolute one the tokens never stated — most often turning `100%` into `100rem`, or an unset value into a guessed default.
1055: +
1056:  **Bad Example**:
1057:  ```markdown
1058:  - Page max-width: 100rem
1059:  ```
1060:  *(tokens.maxContentWidth is `100%`)*
1061: +
1062:  **Why It's Wrong**: `100%` and `100rem` are different layout behaviors. Inventing the concrete value silently changes the design. In v3 this class is structurally prevented for the pre-rendered sections (the formatters emit the verbatim token), so any invented value appears in the AI's prose — exactly where the FACTS block should have been copied. `validate.ts checkQuickStartFidelity` also fails when Quick Start `--page-max-width` disagrees with `tokens.maxContentWidth`.
1063: +
1064:  **Correct Approach**:
1065:  ```markdown
1066:  - Page max-width: 100% (full-bleed; no fixed maximum)
1067:  ```
1068:  Copy the token verbatim, including relative or percentage units. If a value is vague, say what it is — never resolve the ambiguity by guessing an absolute.
1069: +
1070:  **Detection**: Compare every value in the AI-written prose against the FACTS block and pre-rendered sections. Any absolute value (px/rem) where the token is relative (`%`, `auto`, `none`) is invention.

804:  **Why It's Wrong**: This describes parameters without identity. The same sentence could describe a healthcare dashboard, a developer tool, or a children's learning platform. Without brand context, the DESIGN.md cannot guide decisions about tone, voice, or component appropriateness.
805: +
806:  **Correct Approach**:
807:  ```markdown
808:  ## Overview
809: @@ -547,12 +665,15 @@ The accent blue-violet (#533afd) anchors interactive elements across a palette
810:  that balances institutional confidence with approachable warmth.
811:  ```
812:  Name the brand, signal the audience, connect visual choices to brand position.
813: +
814:  **Detection**: Check the opening section for a company/product name and at least one audience or market-position signal. If both are absent, flag AP-21.
815:  
816:  ---
817:  
818:  ### AP-22: Generic Voice
819: +
820:  **Description**: Using casual, enthusiastic, or Silicon Valley-default copy conventions for brands where they are inappropriate.
821: +
822:  **Bad Example**:
823:  ```markdown
824:  ## Content & Voice
825: @@ -561,7 +682,9 @@ Name the brand, signal the audience, connect visual choices to brand position.
826:  - Empty state: "Nothing here yet! Start creating ✨"
827:  ```
828:  *(For a Japanese utility company's customer portal)*
829: +
830:  **Why It's Wrong**: Exclamation marks, emoji, and casual contractions violate the formality expectations of the brand's audience and market. A utility company in Japan communicating with residential customers requires institutional respect, not startup enthusiasm.
831: +
832:  **Correct Approach**:
833:  ```markdown
834:  ## Content & Voice
835: @@ -571,12 +694,15 @@ Name the brand, signal the audience, connect visual choices to brand position.
836:  - Tone: Formal, respectful, institutional. No emoji. No exclamation marks in UI text.
837:  ```
838:  Derive voice from the brand's actual UI text, not from Western SaaS conventions.
839: +
840:  **Detection**: Compare button text and microcopy against the identified brand category. Flag if casual/enthusiastic copy appears for formal/institutional brands.
841:  
842:  ---
843:  
844:  ### AP-23: No Accessibility Contract
845: +
846:  **Description**: Documenting colors, typography, and components without stating WCAG conformance level, contrast ratios, focus specifications, or touch target requirements.
847: +
848:  **Bad Example**:
849:  ```markdown
850:  ## Color Palette
851: @@ -587,7 +713,9 @@ Derive voice from the brand's actual UI text, not from Western SaaS conventions.
852:  | Accent     | #3b82f6 |
853:  ```
854:  *(No contrast ratios, no WCAG level, no focus ring spec)*
855: +
856:  **Why It's Wrong**: `#6b7280` on `#ffffff` has a contrast ratio of 4.6:1, which barely passes WCAG AA for normal text but fails for large text expectations that many teams apply universally. Without stating the ratio, implementers cannot evaluate compliance.
857: +
858:  **Correct Approach**:
859:  ```markdown
860:  ## Color Palette
861: @@ -601,19 +729,24 @@ Derive voice from the brand's actual UI text, not from Western SaaS conventions.
862:  - Focus ring: 2px solid #3b82f6, 2px offset
863:  - Minimum touch target: 44x44px
864:  ```
865: +
866:  **Detection**: Search for "WCAG", "contrast", "focus ring", "touch target" in the document. If none are present, flag AP-23.
867:  
868:  ---
869:  
870:  ### AP-24: State Blindness
871: +
872:  **Description**: Documenting only the default/resting state of components, ignoring loading, empty, error, disabled, and success states.
873: +
874:  **Bad Example**:
875:  ```markdown
876:  ## Data Table
877:  Background: #ffffff | Header: #f9fafb | Border: 1px solid #e5e7eb
878:  Row text: 14px Inter weight 400 | Header text: 12px weight 600 uppercase
879:  ```
880: +
881:  **Why It's Wrong**: A data table is empty when filtered results return nothing, loading when fetching, errored when the API fails, and may show selected rows. Documenting only the data-present state means implementers will invent the other states, creating visual inconsistency.
882: +
883:  **Correct Approach**:
884:  ```markdown
885:  ## Data Table
886: @@ -626,19 +759,24 @@ Row text: 14px Inter weight 400 | Header text: 12px weight 600 uppercase
887:  | Row hover | Background #f9fafb |
888:  | Row selected | Background #eff6ff, left border 2px solid #3b82f6 |
889:  ```
890: +
891:  **Detection**: For each interactive or data-dependent component, check for at least 3 states beyond default. If only the default state is documented, flag AP-24.
892:  
893:  ---
894:  
895:  ### AP-25: Unnamed Principles
896: +
897:  **Description**: Describing what the system does technically without naming the design principle behind the decision.
898: +
899:  **Bad Example**:
900:  ```markdown
901:  ## Shadows
902:  The system uses blue-tinted shadows with rgba(50,50,93,0.25) instead of
903:  standard black shadows.
904:  ```
905: +
906:  **Why It's Wrong**: The observation is correct but unmemorable. Without a name, the principle cannot be referenced in code reviews, design critiques, or component discussions. It becomes a floating fact instead of a system concept.
907: +
908:  **Correct Approach**:
909:  ```markdown
910:  ## Shadows
911: @@ -648,18 +786,23 @@ navy (`rgba(50,50,93,0.25)`), creating shadows that feel integrated with the
912:  palette rather than generically applied.
913:  ```
914:  Name the principle in bold on first use. Reference it by name in subsequent sections.
915: +
916:  **Detection**: Check the atmosphere, shadow, typography, and color sections for bold-formatted principle names. If no section contains a named principle, flag AP-25.
917:  
918:  ---
919:  
920:  ### AP-26: Convention Assumption
921: +
922:  **Description**: Documenting a system's choices without contrasting them with the typical approach, leaving the reader unable to understand what makes this system distinctive.
923: +
924:  **Bad Example**:
925:  ```markdown
926:  ## Typography
927:  Headlines use weight 300 at 48px with -2.4px letter-spacing.
928:  ```
929: +
930:  **Why It's Wrong**: The reader has no frame of reference. They do not know that weight 300 for headlines is unusual (most systems use 600-700), or that -2.4px letter-spacing is extreme (most systems use -0.5px to -1px). Without the contrast, the distinctive choices feel like arbitrary parameters.
931: +
932:  **Correct Approach**:
933:  ```markdown
934:  ## Typography
935: @@ -670,12 +813,15 @@ aggressive than the typical -0.5px to -1px, creating text that feels
936:  compressed and infrastructure-like.
937:  ```
938:  State the convention, then state how this system departs from it.
939: +
940:  **Detection**: Check for comparative language ("unlike", "where most", "rather than", "instead of", "the conventional") in the atmosphere and typography sections. If none appears in a document with distinctive choices, flag AP-26.
941:  
942:  ---
943:  
944:  ### AP-27: Frequency Ignorance
945: +
946:  **Description**: Documenting colors, shadows, or radius values without indicating which ones dominate the system and which are rare exceptions.
947: +
948:  **Bad Example**:
949:  ```markdown
950:  ## Colors
951: @@ -684,7 +830,9 @@ State the convention, then state how this system departs from it.
952:  - #fafafa — surface
953:  - #e5e7eb — border
954:  ```
955: +
956:  **Why It's Wrong**: This flat list implies all four colors have equal importance. In reality, `#171717` may appear on 62% of text elements while `#5e6ad2` appears on only 3%. Without frequency, a developer might use the accent color as freely as the text color, breaking the system's restraint.
957: +
958:  **Correct Approach**:
959:  ```markdown
960:  ## Colors
961: @@ -694,12 +842,15 @@ State the convention, then state how this system departs from it.
962:  - #5e6ad2 — accent [rare: 3% of elements, reserved for interactive states]
963:  ```
964:  Frequency data transforms a color list into a usage strategy.
965: +
966:  **Detection**: Check the color section for frequency indicators (percentage, rank, tier like dominant/common/rare, or usage count). If no color has frequency data, flag AP-27.
967:  
968:  ---
969:  
970:  ### AP-28: Emoji in Formal Brand
971: +
972:  **Description**: Including emoji in copy guidelines, empty states, or error messages for a brand whose tone is formal, institutional, or conservative.
973: +
974:  **Bad Example**:
975:  ```markdown
976:  ## Content Voice
977: @@ -708,7 +859,9 @@ Frequency data transforms a color list into a usage strategy.
978:  - Empty: "No projects yet ✨ Create your first one!"
979:  ```
980:  *(For a B2B financial services platform)*
981: +
982:  **Why It's Wrong**: Emoji in a financial services context undermines the institutional trust the brand requires. The extracted UI text contained zero emoji, but the LLM added them from training data defaults.
983: +
984:  **Correct Approach**:
985:  ```markdown
986:  ## Content Voice
987: @@ -718,18 +871,29 @@ Frequency data transforms a color list into a usage strategy.
988:  - Empty: "No projects found. Create a new project to get started."
989:  ```
990:  Match the emoji policy to the brand's observed behavior. If the source contains no emoji, the output must contain no emoji.
991: +
992:  **Detection**: If the brand is classified as formal/institutional and the document contains emoji in copy examples, flag AP-28. Also flag if the extracted source text contains zero emoji but the output introduces them.

996: +### AP-29: Interpretive Fabrication
997: +
998: +No prose asserts a relationship, cause, consistency, or named principle absent from `tokens.json`. Canonical failures: "gradient-as-depth replaces shadow elevation" (zero shadow/gradient tokens supporting it) and "focus indicators are consistent" (no captured focus styles). 1003: +
1004:  **Description**: Printing raw frequency or usage-count data in the output prose or tables ("border 9685, text 4258", "appears on 62% of elements", "47 occurrences").

1006:  **Bad Example**:

1018:  | Voltage | `#5e6ad2` | `--color-voltage` | Interactive elements only |

1020:  Express frequency as ROLE and ordering: the dominant colour is "primary text", the rare one carries an "interactive elements only" guard.
1021: +
1022:  **Detection**: Flag any number that is a count or percentage of usage (e.g. `\d{3,}` next to a colour, `\d+%` of elements, "N occurrences"). Frequency figures do not belong in the output.

1026:  ### AP-31: Placeholder Labels (div / Variant-N) (v3)
1027: +
1028:  **Description**: Carrying the extractor's raw DOM tags ("div", "span") or auto-indexed labels ("Variant-1", "Color 2") into the named Style Reference.

1030:  **Bad Example**:

1033: @@ -752,7 +919,9 @@ Express frequency as ROLE and ordering: the dominant colour is "primary text", t

1036:  ```
1037: +
1038:  **Why It's Wrong**: "Variant-1" and "div" are extractor internals, not design names. A v3 Style Reference is a named handoff: every component is named by function and every type role is semantic. Placeholder labels make the doc unusable as a reference and signal the agent stopped at transcription.
1039: +
1040:  **Correct Approach**:
1041:  ```markdown

1044:  **Role:** Low-emphasis inline action — `#2564eb` text, no fill.
1045:  ```

1052:  ### AP-32: Value Invention from a Vague Token (v3)
1053: +
1054:  **Description**: Concretizing a vague or relative token value into a specific absolute one the tokens never stated — most often turning `100%` into `100rem`, or an unset value into a guessed default.
1055: +
1056:  **Bad Example**:

1061: +

1064:  **Correct Approach**:
1065:  ```markdown

1067:  ```

1069: +
1070:  **Detection**: Compare every value in the AI-written prose against the FACTS block and pre-rendered sections. Any absolute value (px/rem) where the token is relative (`%`, `auto`, `none`) is invention.

- The surface in scope: a component, a screen, a described complaint, or a set of files to review.
- Optionally, an existing token file, design system, or a measured `DESIGN.md` Style Reference. Any of these **outranks** this skill's defaults.

### Outputs

- Concrete values and CSS, plus the reason each value was chosen from its scale.
- For an improve task, the symptom-to-cause mapping that justified each change.
- For a review, severity-tiered findings with file, line and fix.

- **`sk-design-md-generator`** measures a live site's real CSS into a v3 Style Reference. It is the reading half of the pair; this skill is the writing half. When a Style Reference exists for the surface, its measured values are ground truth and this skill supplies only what the reference left undecided.
- **`sk-code`** implements the result. Hand it the chosen values, not adjectives.
- **`system-spec-kit`** owns packet documentation and continuity when the work is tracked.

1: ---
2: title: Numeric Design Laws
3: description: A stable, citable index of numeric design thresholds for contrast, motion, spacing, type, and neutral color, used when a reference finding depends on a number.
4: trigger_phrases:
5:   - "numeric design laws"
6:   - "design thresholds"
7:   - "contrast motion spacing type thresholds"
8: importance_tier: normal

10: version: 1.0.0.0
11: ---
12: 
13: # Numeric Design Laws
14: 
15: A condensed index of numeric design thresholds for contrast, motion, spacing, type, and neutral color. Each row gives a stable value to cite when reading an extracted surface, so a finding can rest on a number instead of a guess.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### Purpose
22: 
23: Give one stable, citable row per numeric threshold instead of re-deriving contrast, motion, spacing, type, and neutral-color values independently when a captured surface is measured.
24: 
25: ### Usage
26: 
27: Cite a row by `law_id` when a finding or observation about an extracted surface depends on a numeric threshold. Values are craft targets, not hard gates in this skill — a captured surface may legitimately differ; the row explains what "on target" means. The values give a Style Reference honest, comparable numbers instead of vague adjectives.
28: 
29: ### Reading Targets, Not Authoring Instructions
30: 
31: Every row here describes a surface that **already exists**. None of them tells anyone what to build. That distinction matters because the sibling skill `sk-design` authors values for surfaces that do not exist yet, and on three rows the two skills would appear to disagree if the direction were ignored.
32: 
33: | Row | Reading here | Authoring in `sk-design` |
34: |---|---|---|
35: | `type-modular-ratio` | Report the ratio a captured type scale expresses | Reject ratios; the type scale is hand-picked, because ratios produce fractional pixels and are too sparse for interface density |
36: | `spacing-scale` | Note whether a captured value resolves to a baseline step | Use the full 16-step scale, where no two neighbours sit closer than about 25% |
37: | The three `motion-*` bands | Describe the timing a captured surface uses | Bands split by kind: 120-180ms direct feedback, 180-260ms state change, up to 500ms layout transition |
38: 
39: A measured ratio is an observation, never an instruction to generate the next size by multiplication. When both skills are in play, this document reports and `sk-design` decides; where a surface has already been measured, its measured values outrank `sk-design`'s defaults. The authoring side states the same reconciliation from its own direction in `sk-design/sk-design-fundamentals/references/motion-principles.md` Section 5 and `sk-design/sk-design-fundamentals/SKILL.md` Section 7. Do not cite a row as a reason to change a design. That is the authoring direction, and it belongs to `sk-design`.
40: 
41: ---
42: 
43: ## 2. LAW INDEX
44: 
45: | law_id | value/range | caveat |
46: |---|---|---|
47: | contrast-body-aa | 4.5:1 WCAG AA body text | Product or regulatory contexts may set a stricter bar; failing body pairs are a real finding. |
48: | contrast-large-ui-aa | 3:1 for large text, icons, visible focus, and UI controls | Applies to large text and non-text UI only; body text still uses 4.5:1. |
49: | contrast-apca-lc | absolute APCA Lc >= 60 where APCA is available | Record APCA alongside WCAG evidence; it does not replace WCAG targets. |
50: | motion-feedback | 100-150 ms for press, hover, tap, and tiny feedback | Under ~80 ms reads as instant; keep near the floor without disappearing. |
51: | motion-state-change | 200-300 ms for toggle, dropdown, tooltip, and tab change | User-initiated feedback over 300 ms feels laggy; use for state changes, not tiny feedback. |
52: | motion-layout-transition | 300-500 ms for modal, drawer, accordion, and layout transition | Similar transitions should share timing so motion explains continuity. |
53: | motion-earned-entrance | 500-800 ms for one earned entrance or brand choreography | One memorable entrance can be earned; repeated page-load choreography is not. |
54: | register-product-motion-budget | 150-250 ms state transitions for Product surfaces | Compresses the Product posture; see `./register.md` Section 3. |
55: | spacing-scale | 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48 px; section spacing clamp(48px, 8vw, 96px) | Captured spacing that does not resolve to a baseline step is a one-off worth noting. |

12: 
13: # Numeric Design Laws
14: 
15: A condensed index of numeric design thresholds for contrast, motion, spacing, type, and neutral color. Each row gives a stable value to cite when reading an extracted surface, so a finding can rest on a number instead of a guess.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### Purpose
22: 
23: Give one stable, citable row per numeric threshold instead of re-deriving contrast, motion, spacing, type, and neutral-color values independently when a captured surface is measured.
24: 
25: ### Usage
26: 
27: Cite a row by `law_id` when a finding or observation about an extracted surface depends on a numeric threshold. Values are craft targets, not hard gates in this skill — a captured surface may legitimately differ; the row explains what "on target" means. The values give a Style Reference honest, comparable numbers instead of vague adjectives.
28: 
29: ### Reading Targets, Not Authoring Instructions
30: 
31: Every row here describes a surface that **already exists**. None of them tells anyone what to build. That distinction matters because the sibling skill `sk-design` authors values for surfaces that do not exist yet, and on three rows the two skills would appear to disagree if the direction were ignored.
32: 
33: | Row | Reading here | Authoring in `sk-design` |
34: |---|---|---|
35: | `type-modular-ratio` | Report the ratio a captured type scale expresses | Reject ratios; the type scale is hand-picked, because ratios produce fractional pixels and are too sparse for interface density |
36: | `spacing-scale` | Note whether a captured value resolves to a baseline step | Use the full 16-step scale, where no two neighbours sit closer than about 25% |
37: | The three `motion-*` bands | Describe the timing a captured surface uses | Bands split by kind: 120-180ms direct feedback, 180-260ms state change, up to 500ms layout transition |
38: 
39: A measured ratio is an observation, never an instruction to generate the next size by multiplication. When both skills are in play, this document reports and `sk-design` decides; where a surface has already been measured, its measured values outrank `sk-design`'s defaults. The authoring side states the same reconciliation from its own direction in `sk-design/sk-design-fundamentals/references/motion-principles.md` Section 5 and `sk-design/sk-design-fundamentals/SKILL.md` Section 7. Do not cite a row as a reason to change a design. That is the authoring direction, and it belongs to `sk-design`.
40: 
41: ---
42: 
43: ## 2. LAW INDEX
44: 
45: | law_id | value/range | caveat |
46: |---|---|---|
47: | contrast-body-aa | 4.5:1 WCAG AA body text | Product or regulatory contexts may set a stricter bar; failing body pairs are a real finding. |
48: | contrast-large-ui-aa | 3:1 for large text, icons, visible focus, and UI controls | Applies to large text and non-text UI only; body text still uses 4.5:1. |
49: | contrast-apca-lc | absolute APCA Lc >= 60 where APCA is available | Record APCA alongside WCAG evidence; it does not replace WCAG targets. |
50: | motion-feedback | 100-150 ms for press, hover, tap, and tiny feedback | Under ~80 ms reads as instant; keep near the floor without disappearing. |
51: | motion-state-change | 200-300 ms for toggle, dropdown, tooltip, and tab change | User-initiated feedback over 300 ms feels laggy; use for state changes, not tiny feedback. |
52: | motion-layout-transition | 300-500 ms for modal, drawer, accordion, and layout transition | Similar transitions should share timing so motion explains continuity. |
53: | motion-earned-entrance | 500-800 ms for one earned entrance or brand choreography | One memorable entrance can be earned; repeated page-load choreography is not. |

21: 
22: ## 1. OVERVIEW
23: 
24: ### Purpose
25: 
26: This document draws the line around the cardinal fidelity rule. It names four origins a value can have, gives each a source-of-truth label, and states plainly which origins this mode is allowed to write.
27: 
28: ### When to Use
29: 
30: - A value's origin is unclear before it enters a token table.
31: - A request asks for a Style Reference from a brief with no live site.
32: - A review or validation finding needs its provenance traced.
33: 
34: ### Core Principle
35: 
36: Read this as a boundary map, not a feature. It adds no new capability and it does not relax the fidelity contract by one digit.
37: 
38: ---
39: 
40: ## 2. WHY THE BOUNDARY EXISTS
41: 
42: A Style Reference is trusted because a reader can assume every hex, pixel, weight, radius and shadow in it was measured from a running page. The moment a value with a different origin slips in unlabeled, that assumption breaks for the whole document and the reader can no longer tell ground truth from a guess.
43: 
44: The risk is not careless invention. It is the quiet drift where a plausible-looking value from a brief or a reasonable inference about direction gets written into a token table as if it were measured. The defense is a clear boundary plus a label on anything that is not a measured value.
45: 
46: This mode captures what already exists. It does not author a design from a brief. Keeping those two jobs separate is what this boundary protects.
47: 
48: ---
49: 
50: ## 3. THE FOUR ORIGINS
51: 
52: Every value a reader might want in a Style Reference comes from one of four origins. The first is the only one this mode writes into token tables.
53: 
54: ### 3.1 Measured
55: 
56: A value read off the running page by the extractor and present in `tokens.json`. Hex codes, pixel sizes, font weights, border radii, box shadows, spacing steps, durations. These are the only values allowed in the Tokens tables, Surfaces, Elevation and the Quick Start blocks. They are copied verbatim, never rounded, never normalized, never concretized.
57: 
58: ### 3.2 Brief-provided
59: 
60: A value the user supplied in the request rather than the site. A stakeholder might say the brand red is a specific hex or that the body font should be a named family, before any extraction confirms it on the page. A brief-provided value is a stated intent, not a measurement. It is not ground truth about the live surface and it never enters a token table as if the extractor found it.
61: 
62: ### 3.3 Inferred
63: 
64: A characterization the writer derives from measured values. Naming a near-black `Obsidian Ink`, stating a color's role, calling the density spacious, listing Similar Brands. These are grounded inferences built on real tokens and the format already allows them. The line is exact: name and characterize what IS measured, never invent a fact, a value or an audience that is not.
65: 
66: ### 3.4 Absent
67: 
68: A value the extractor did not capture. No dark palette, no shadow tokens, no imagery signal, no accessibility data. Absent is a real state with a real treatment in the format. A section with no backing data is omitted when conditional or stamped that no data was extracted. Absent is never filled by reaching for a brief-provided guess or by deriving a value the page never showed.
69: 
70: ---
71: 
72: ## 4. SOURCE-OF-TRUTH LABELS
73: 
74: Labels keep the four origins legible inside one document so the cardinal rule stays enforceable by inspection.
75: 
76: | Origin | Label in the document | Where it may appear |
77: |---|---|---|
78: | Measured | unlabeled, the default | Token tables, Surfaces, Elevation, Quick Start, characterizing prose |
79: | Brief-provided | stated as the brief's intent, never as a token | Prose context only, kept out of value tables |
80: | Inferred | `[INFERRED]` and cites the measured token it rests on | Names, roles, Similar Brands, characterizing prose |
81: | Absent | stamped that no data was extracted or the section omitted | The section that would have held the value |
82: 
83: Three rules govern the labels.
84: 
85: 1. Measured is the default and carries no label. Because it is the default, anything that is NOT measured has to be marked, so an unlabeled value is a promise that the extractor measured it.
86: 2. A brief-provided value never sits in a token table. It is not a measurement and the table is reserved for measurements. If a brief value needs recording, it belongs in prose as a stated intent, plainly distinct from the measured tokens.
87: 3. An inferred claim names what is measured and cites the token under it. Inference characterizes real data. It never manufactures a value, and the citation is what lets a reader trace it back to ground truth.
88: 
89: ---
90: 
91: ## 5. WHAT THIS MODE WRITES
92: 
93: This mode writes measured values and grounded inferences about them. Nothing else reaches a token table.
94: 
95: - Measured values fill the Tokens tables, Surfaces, Elevation and the Quick Start, verbatim from `tokens.json`.
96: - Inferences supply evocative names, plain role statements and Similar Brands, each grounded in a measured token.
97: - Brief-provided values stay out of the value tables. They may set context in prose as a stated intent and they never wear the appearance of a measurement.
98: - Absent values are stamped or omitted, never backfilled.
99: 
100: The Quick Start exists because the output is ship-ready, and it is ship-ready precisely because every value in it was measured. A brief-provided or invented value in the Quick Start would hand a coding agent a fabricated token under the banner of ground truth, which is the exact failure the cardinal rule exists to prevent.
101: 
102: ---
103: 
104: ## 6. FORWARD-AUTHORING IS OUT OF SCOPE
105: 
106: Generating a Style Reference from a brief alone, with no live site to measure, is forward-authoring. It is OUT OF SCOPE for this mode and this document does not enable it.
107: 
108: Forward-authoring inverts the input contract. This mode starts from a running page and reports what is measurably there. Forward-authoring starts from a brief and proposes what should be there. A skill in the wider field, the Stitch design-taste skill, illustrates the forward-authoring shape: it turns a vibe and a set of directives into a `DESIGN.md` for screen generation with no extraction step and no measured source. That is a different job with a different contract, and treating its output and this mode's output as interchangeable is the category error this boundary guards against.
109: 
110: The reasons forward-authoring stays out are structural, not a matter of effort.
111: 
112: - Different input contract. Measured extraction needs a live, renderable URL. Forward-authoring needs only a brief. Folding both into one mode would blur the very assumption that makes a Style Reference trustworthy.
113: - Fidelity must not weaken. The cardinal rule binds every value to `tokens.json`. A brief-driven path has no `tokens.json` to bind to, so admitting it here would force a relaxation of the contract. That trade is refused.
114: - No second backend. This mode already extracts, writes, validates and reports through one pipeline. Forward-authoring is not a missing stage of that pipeline. It is a separate capability.
115: 
116: When a user wants a design authored from a brief with no site to measure, that is the sibling authoring skill `sk-design`, routed away from this mode.
117: 
118: - Do not satisfy the request by loosening fidelity here.
119: - Do not produce any part of a Style Reference artifact as a consolation output: no Tokens table, no Surfaces, no Quick Start, not even with brief values labeled or a disclaimer sentence attached.
120: - A labeled or disclaimed artifact is still forward-authoring; this boundary forbids the artifact itself, not just unlabeled values inside it.
121: - The entire response is text: either a request for the live URL, or an explicit statement that this mode captures an existing surface and brief-only authoring is a different contract handled elsewhere, citing this document (`references/authoring-boundary.md`) and `assets/source-of-truth-router-card.md` by path so the boundary decision is traceable in what the user sees, not just in tool-call history.
122: 
123: ---
124: 
125: ## 7. QUICK BOUNDARY CHECK
126: 
127: Run this before writing any value into a Style Reference.
128: 
129: ```text
130: □ Is the value in tokens.json? If yes, it is measured. Copy it verbatim, no label.
131: □ Did it come from the brief, not the page? Keep it out of token tables. Note it as intent in prose only.
132: □ Is it a characterization of a measured value? Mark it [INFERRED] and cite the token.
133: □ Did the extractor not capture it? Stamp the section absent or omit it. Never backfill.
134: □ Are you authoring from a brief with no live site? Stop before writing anything — no Tokens table, no partial artifact, not even one labeled value. Ask for the live URL, or state the out-of-scope routing decision, citing this document and the router card by path in your response text.
135: ```
136: 
137: ---
138: 
139: ## 8. RELATED RESOURCES
140: 
141: - [design-md-format.md](design-md-format.md) - the Style Reference section specification and the Section 0 cardinal rules this boundary protects.
142: - [../assets/source-of-truth-router-card.md](../assets/source-of-truth-router-card.md) - the fill-in card that sorts each value into measured, brief-provided, inferred or absent before writing.
143: - [../assets/cardinal-rules-card.md](../assets/cardinal-rules-card.md) - the pre-validate fidelity checklist.
144: - [design-knowledge/register.md](design-knowledge/register.md) - the Brand-vs-Product register. This mode records the extracted surface's register, it does not author one from a brief.

17: # Design System Documentation Quality Checklist
18: 
19: Use this checklist to validate every generated design system document before delivery. Each item includes verification steps, common failure modes, and fixes.
20: 
21: ---
22: 
23: ## 1. OVERVIEW
24: 
25: The current output is the v3 **Style Reference** (`design-md-format.md`): a named, confident, restrained design-system handoff whose value-bearing sections (`## Tokens — Colors`, `## Tokens — Spacing & Shapes`, `## Surfaces`, `## Quick Start`) are pre-rendered deterministically by `backend/scripts/formatters-v3.ts` and pasted unchanged. The agent writes prose only. Many checks below therefore verify that the pre-rendered sections were not edited and that the prose is named, grounded, and honest.
26: 
27: **Named, deterministic, and honest.**
28: 
29: - Colours are NAMED evocatively (Obsidian Ink, Voltage) with clean `--color-<slug>` tokens; components are NAMED by function (Primary CTA, Card, Badge), never "Variant-N" or "div".
30: - Because the value tables are pre-rendered, value-fidelity failures mean the block was edited after pasting — restore it.
31: - The Quick Start is checked by `checkQuickStartFidelity` (every hex traces to a token; `--page-max-width` matches `tokens.maxContentWidth`).
32: - Elevation is never omitted — when 0 shadows it is rendered FLAT and the prose states how depth is achieved (border contrast, whitespace), never "gradient-as-depth".
33: 
34: **Data-driven, not fabrication-driven.** Conditional sections (e.g. Imagery) are gated on token presence. When a section has no backing token data, stamp it ABSENT (`_No <X> data was extracted._`) — never invent content, a minimum count, comparative framing, or a named principle to fill it. "All sections present and non-empty" is a data-driven expectation, not a mandate to fabricate.
35: 
36: - Every interpretive claim must cite a token or be labelled `[INFERRED]`.
37: - `validate.ts` enforces this with prose-discipline and section-coverage checks (both WARNING-tier) and reports a dual score — `valuesScore` (hex/section/format fidelity) and `claimsScore` (prose provenance).
38: - `isValidationPass` passes only with zero hard failures in the `target`, `schema` and `provenance` categories.
39: - The dual score is printed for information and does not decide the verdict.
40: 
41: ---
42:

17: # Design System Documentation Quality Checklist
18: 
19: Use this checklist to validate every generated design system document before delivery. Each item includes verification steps, common failure modes, and fixes.
20: 
21: ---
22: 
23: ## 1. OVERVIEW
24: 
25: The current output is the v3 **Style Reference** (`design-md-format.md`): a named, confident, restrained design-system handoff whose value-bearing sections (`## Tokens — Colors`, `## Tokens — Spacing & Shapes`, `## Surfaces`, `## Quick Start`) are pre-rendered deterministically by `backend/scripts/formatters-v3.ts` and pasted unchanged. The agent writes prose only. Many checks below therefore verify that the pre-rendered sections were not edited and that the prose is named, grounded, and honest.
26: 
27: **Named, deterministic, and honest.**
28: 
29: - Colours are NAMED evocatively (Obsidian Ink, Voltage) with clean `--color-<slug>` tokens; components are NAMED by function (Primary CTA, Card, Badge), never "Variant-N" or "div".
30: - Because the value tables are pre-rendered, value-fidelity failures mean the block was edited after pasting — restore it.
31: - The Quick Start is checked by `checkQuickStartFidelity` (every hex traces to a token; `--page-max-width` matches `tokens.maxContentWidth`).
32: - Elevation is never omitted — when 0 shadows it is rendered FLAT and the prose states how depth is achieved (border contrast, whitespace), never "gradient-as-depth".
33: 
34: **Data-driven, not fabrication-driven.** Conditional sections (e.g. Imagery) are gated on token presence. When a section has no backing token data, stamp it ABSENT (`_No <X> data was extracted._`) — never invent content, a minimum count, comparative framing, or a named principle to fill it. "All sections present and non-empty" is a data-driven expectation, not a mandate to fabricate.
35: 
36: - Every interpretive claim must cite a token or be labelled `[INFERRED]`.
37: - `validate.ts` enforces this with prose-discipline and section-coverage checks (both WARNING-tier) and reports a dual score — `valuesScore` (hex/section/format fidelity) and `claimsScore` (prose provenance).
38: - `isValidationPass` passes only with zero hard failures in the `target`, `schema` and `provenance` categories.
39: - The dual score is printed for information and does not decide the verdict.

14: # Skill Reference File Templates - AI Agent Skills
15: 
16: Templates for creating reference files in AI agent skills with deep-dive technical guidance.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Location & Naming
23: 
24: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`
25: 
26: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only
27: 
28: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
29: |---------------|-----------------|
30: | `implementation-workflows.md` | `ImplementationWorkflows.md` (PascalCase) |
31: | `tool-catalog.md` | `tool_catalog.md` (snake_case) |
32: | `debugging-guide.md` | `DebuggingGuide.MD` (wrong case) |
33: | `quick-reference.md` | `quickReference.md` (camelCase) |
34: | `code-quality-standards.md` | `code quality standards.md` (spaces) |
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
69: 
70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95: 
96: #### BAD Intro Structure (duplicates content)
97: 
98: ```markdown
99: # Git Commit Workflows
100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
104: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Intro vs Section 1 Content Placement
121: 
122: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | Section 1 OVERVIEW |
123: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
124: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat) |
125: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
126: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
127: | Primary Sources       | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (as "Key Sources") |
128: | Purpose (detailed)    | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
129: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
130: | Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |
131: 
132: ---
133: 
134: ### Reference Body Skeleton
135: 
136: **Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.
137: 
138: ```markdown
139: # [Title]
140: 
141: [1-2 sentence hook: what this reference covers and when to reach for it.]
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 1. OVERVIEW
146: 
147: ### Purpose
148: 
149: [The outcome this reference produces, in one or two sentences.]
150: 
151: ### When to Use
152: 
153: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
154: - [Second trigger]
155: 
156: ### Core Principle
157: 
158: [One-line statement that governs every rule below.]
159: 
160: ### Boundaries
161: 
162: - **In scope**: [What this reference owns]
163: - **Out of scope**: [What belongs in a sibling reference]
164: 
165: ### Key Sources
166: 
167: - [title](url) - [What the source establishes]
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 2. [CONTENT SECTION]
172: 
173: ### [Rule Group]
174: 
175: - **Rule:** [What to do]
176: - **Why:** [The failure it prevents]
177: - **Check:** [How to verify it]
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 3. [CONTENT SECTION]
182: 
183: [Body of the section]
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 4. RELATED RESOURCES
188: 
189: - [title](./sibling-reference.md) - [What the reader gets there]
190: ```
191: 
192: **Rules the skeleton encodes:**
193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.
194: - Content sections use integer numbers only: `## 2.`, `## 3.`, and so on.
195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.
197: - Every `---` has a blank line above it, so a divider never turns the line above into a setext heading.
198: - A related section, when present, is the last H2.
